lesson.title: The One Number That Predicts a Reaction: Gibbs Free Energy
lesson.summary: Gibbs free energy combines a system's enthalpy and entropy into a single quantity that predicts whether a biological reaction can occur spontaneously, making it the practical bridge between the abstract laws of thermodynamics and real cellular chemistry.
lesson.body:
The first law says energy is conserved, the second law says entropy tends to increase, and entropy itself measures how many arrangements are available to a system. Useful as those ideas are individually, none of them alone answers the question a cell actually needs answered constantly: will this specific reaction happen on its own, right now, under these conditions? Gibbs free energy, named after physicist Josiah Willard Gibbs and usually written as G, is the quantity built specifically to answer that question by folding energy and entropy together into one number.

The defining relationship is G equals H minus TS, where H is enthalpy, essentially the total heat content of the system, T is the absolute temperature, and S is entropy. What matters for predicting a reaction is not the absolute value of G but the change in G, written delta G, as reactants turn into products. Delta G equals the change in enthalpy minus the temperature multiplied by the change in entropy. This single expression captures both thermodynamic laws at once: the enthalpy term tracks energy the way the first law demands, and the entropy term tracks the second law's dispersal tendency, both weighted appropriately by temperature.

The sign of delta G is what determines whether a reaction is spontaneous. A negative delta G means the products have less free energy than the reactants, so the reaction releases usable energy and can proceed on its own without an external energy input, a category called exergonic. A positive delta G means the products have more free energy than the reactants, so the reaction requires an input of energy to proceed and will not happen spontaneously, called endergonic. A delta G of zero describes a system at equilibrium, where the forward and reverse reactions are balanced and there is no net driving force in either direction.

The breakdown of glucose during cellular respiration is a useful concrete case. Glucose has substantially higher free energy than the carbon dioxide and water it is broken down into, so the overall process has a strongly negative delta G, meaning it is thermodynamically favorable and releases a large amount of usable energy, much of which the cell captures by generating ATP rather than losing it all as heat. Note that a negative delta G only says a reaction can happen spontaneously, not that it will happen quickly. Glucose sitting in a jar on a shelf does not spontaneously combust into carbon dioxide and water even though the thermodynamics favor it, because the reaction faces a large energy barrier that has to be overcome first, which is exactly why cells rely on enzymes to speed reactions up without changing whether they are thermodynamically favorable in the first place.

Free energy is also what makes it possible for cells to run reactions that would otherwise never happen on their own. An endergonic reaction with a positive delta G can still occur if it is directly coupled to a strongly exergonic reaction, most often the hydrolysis of ATP, so that the combined delta G of the two reactions together is negative. This coupling strategy, using a very favorable reaction to drag an unfavorable one along with it, is one of the central organizing principles of cellular metabolism, and it depends entirely on being able to add and compare free energy changes the way delta G allows.
